display_title: Official Review of Submission6450 by Reviewer RfGj

summary.value:
The paper addresses an important challenge in post-training quantization (PTQ) for large language models: conventional methods quantize each linear layer by minimizing the immediate activation error locally, without considering how that rounding propagates through subsequent layers and affects the overall model output distribution. The authors propose YAQA (Yet Another Quantization Algorithm), a two-part adaptive rounding method: (1) they compute Kronecker-factored approximations of each layer’s Hessian of the full-model Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss; (2) they use these sketches in a rounding algorithm with theoretical guarantees. It combines A "Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation" to efficiently estimate model sensitivity, and  an "adaptive rounding algorithm" that minimizes quantization error with respect to the full-model KL divergence.  

The approach maintains model fidelity more effectively than standard PTQ, achieving up to 30% lower KL divergence and improved downstream performance on large language models. 

My recommendation is to accept this paper provided Authors are able to demonstrate that this method can be extended to other important layers of transformers.

strengths.value:
* Proposes a new quantization formulation that minimizes the KL divergence between the original and quantized model outputs, instead of per-layer reconstruction errors. This supposedly produces a better quantized model (also supported by experiments) 
* Introduces a Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation (\(H_O \otimes H_I\)) to capture second-order information efficiently for large-scale networks.
* Develops an adaptive rounding method that minimizes a Hessian-weighted quadratic error function, providing better alignment between quantized and original weights.
* Derives theoretical error bounds for the rounding objective and proposes incoherence transformations (e.g., Hadamard transforms) to reduce approximation bias.
* Ensures compatibility with multiple quantization schemes (INT4, INT8, mixed precision) without retraining or model-specific fine-tuning.
* Demonstrates significant improvements in KL divergence and downstream metrics on large language models (e.g., LLaMA-family) compared to existing PTQ baselines (CBQ, LDLQ etc) .

weaknesses.value:
* The method relies on the Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation \(H_O \otimes H_I\) which is generally efficient, it is still an approximation and the performance depends heavily on how accurately it captures the true curvature of the loss.  The sensitivity of results to sketch quality, dataset size, or model architecture is underexplored.

* Estimating Hessian sketches (via power iterations or data sampling) adds computational cost compared to simple rounding which can have implication on runtime and memory overhead, especially for very large LLMs and this needs to be quantified. 
* The algorithm mainly targets linear (fully-connected) layers.  It may not generalize directly to non-linear components such as attention modules, normalization layers, or activation quantization. Although linear layers are significant part of these models, attention needs to be tackled for a meaningful conclusion. 
* Experiments are focused on LLMs and it would have been better to add more tasks such as vision to see if the idea has benefit in other domains
* While the paper focuses on post-training quantization (PTQ), comparing against quantization-aware training (QAT) baselines would clarify the performance gap and practical trade-offs. 
* Some critical implementation details — such as hyperparameter settings, sketching configurations, or data requirements — are not fully described.  Authors are encouraged to provide more details.

questions.value:
* What are hyperparameter settings, sketching configurations etc.? /
* Can Authors provide comparison of end to end model performance compared to any QAT method such as LSQ?

comment.value:
- The method relies on the Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation ...
  - **Figure 3 in the paper shows an empirical evaluation of the sketch quality, and Tables 1 and 4 in the paper show the effect of these variations on empirical quantization quality.** 
- Estimating Hessian sketches (via power iterations or data sampling) ...
  - **Lines 300-301 and 315-316 in the paper give concrete numbers for the cost of obtaining Hessians. Section A.2 in the Appendix contains an analysis of the number of FLOPs needed for each Hessian sketch.** The cost of quantization (i.e. running the fixed point iteration) is higher than LDLQ due to the higher SND, but both are negligible in practice (under a minute per linear layer for a 8B model with an unoptimized implementation). A single set of Hessians for a model can also be reused across different quantizations of the same model, amortizing cost.
  - **It is important to note that in practice, the cost of quantization is usually not a factor in deciding which quantized model to deploy. Quantized models reap savings every time they are run, whereas quantization is a one-time fixed overhead cost.** Choosing the highest quality quantized model for a target size is more important than saving cost up front, which is one reason why people use QAT in practice despite it costing much more than PTQ.
- The algorithm mainly targets linear (fully-connected) layers...
  - **Over 95% of the weights in modern LLMs are in linear layers. As such, essentially all real-world quantized models only quantize linear layers.** Layernorms hold an epsilon number of parameters, and activation quantization is a somewhat orthogonal problem to weight quantization. This paper focuses on weight-only quantization, although it could probably be applied to weight-activation quantization as well (in the same way that QuaRot and SpinQuant both use GPTQ to round weights in their larger weight-activation quantization frameworks).
  - **Quantizing the attention operation is also a completely orthogonal problem to quantizing the weights in order to compress a model. It is unreasonable to expect a weight-only LLM quantization paper to cover quantizing the attention operation, and to the best of our knowledge, no paper in the literature does this (including none of our baselines).** The point of quantized attention is to use low precision datatypes when computing $qk^T$ and to compress the KV cache, whereas the point of quantizing the weights of a model is to reduce the IO volume needed for memory-bound settings or for potential use with low precision datatypes in compute-bound settings.
- Experiments are focused on LLMs and it would have been better to add more tasks such as vision to see if the idea has benefit in other domains
  - **This is a weight-only LLM quantization paper. It was advertised as such, so we do not know why you would expect to find experiments on (comparatively tiny) vision models. LLM quantization is its own subfield, and no noteworthy method in the literature runs experiments on both LLMs and pure vision models, because vision models are not LLMs.** 
- While the paper focuses on post-training quantization (PTQ), comparing against quantization-aware training (QAT) baselines would clarify the performance gap and practical trade-offs.
  - **Table 3 and Section 4.1.1 in the paper contain a comparison against QAT baselines. In particular, YAQA achieves a lower KL divergence than Google’s QAT Gemma 3 model, which was produced by a leading industry lab (namely, Google).**
- Some critical implementation details — such as hyperparameter settings, sketching configurations, or data requirements — are not fully described. Authors are encouraged to provide more details.
  - **These details are all in the Appendix.** If we missed anything, please let us know.
- What are hyperparameter settings, sketching configurations etc.? /
  - **See the Appendix.**
- Can Authors provide comparison of end to end model performance compared to any QAT method such as LSQ?
  - **We already did. See Table 3 and Section 4.1.1.** From our understanding, **LSQ is an older method from 2019 that was tested and designed for vision models**, which makes it hard to compare against. However, **our chosen QAT baseline, Google’s QAT Gemma 3, is from 2025 and was designed for LLMs, making it a clear modern baseline**. As Table 3 and Section 4.1.1 show, **YAQA does a better job of preserving the original model than Google’s QAT recipe.**

comment.value:
> This is just to check the generalizability of a method which supposedly has good merit. I do not see any reason why it can be just limited to LLMs.

There are a few main reasons why we did not evaluate YAQA on traditional pure vision models in this paper. YAQA quantizes linear layers in a model, so for YAQA to be worth applying, a model should be sufficiently large and have a large proportion of its parameters in linear layers. In the current state of machine learning, the main models that satisfy this are LLMs and other large transformers. In contrast, most non transformer-based vision models such as ResNets use convolutional layers, which are fundamentally different with respect to quantization. While it is probably possible to adapt the concepts of YAQA to quantizing convolutional layers, this is beyond the scope of this work.

There are some pure vision models such as ViT's and Swin Transformers that do have lots of linear layers because they are based on transformers. **However, these models are comparatively tiny, with most only having O(100M) parameters.** As such, the vision transformer quantization community has developed a large corpus of literature that takes advantage of this size by using advanced techniques such as knowledge distillation, complex QAT, and better Hessian estimates. **Many of these methods are too expensive to scale to O(100B) parameter LLMs that are over 1000X larger than these vision models.** LLM quantization methods (including QAT methods) are designed to both achieve high quality while being scalable to large models, making a direct comparison to vision quantization methods that assume a much higher compute budget relative to the model size difficult and unfair. As empirical evidence, the largest ViT seems to be Google's ViT 22B model, and the largest Swin Transformer seems to be the 3B parameter Swin Transformer V2 model, both of which came out around 3 years ago. We were unable to find any works in the literature that have quantized these models, even among the latest vision quantization papers that came out this year. 

We'd also like to point out that none of the LLM quantization papers in the literature evaluate performance on vision models (including vision transformers), probably because of the exact reasons we pointed out. **Key papers in the field such as GPTQ, QuIP, QuIP#, QTIP, NestQuant, SmoothQuant, AWQ, SpinQuant, QuaRot, OmniQuant, CBQ, AQLM, and PV-Tuning, all of which have been accepted to top conferences and many of which have won awards, *all do not compare to vision models*.** If you'd like to suggest a large vision model (>>1B parameters) with lots of linear layers that existing SOTA quantization methods have been tested on, we would be willing to attempt to quantize it. However, due to there only being a few days left in the discussion period, we make no promises that we can finish this task before the deadline.

> I could all these details.

Did you miss a word here? If you couldn't find a certain detail, please let us know what is missing so we can add it.

display_title: Official Review of Submission6450 by Reviewer odoJ

summary.value: This paper proposes YAQA (Yet Another Quantization Algorithm), a quantization method that directly optimizes end-to-end model error via a Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation, providing the first theoretical bounds on quantization error while preserving model behavior without affecting inference efficiency.

strengths.value:
1. YAQA provides the first formal end-to-end quantization error bounds, linking quantization quality directly to the cosine similarity between the true and approximated Hessians.
2. Built on a Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation, YAQA is compatible with various quantizers and maintains the same computational complexity as prior adaptive rounding methods
3. It introduces symmetric input–output feedback and structured Hessian forms, ensuring faster convergence and greater rounding stability

weaknesses.value:
1. Is the Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation transferable across different model architectures?
2. Can the “structural nilpotence degree” quantitatively predict convergence speed in real applications?
3. Can the proposed method be applied to mixed-precision quantization?
4. The paper claims that the proposed method introduces no additional inference overhead — could the authors provide supporting evidence or justification for this claim?
5. The advantage of YAQA appears to mainly arise from its more accurate Hessian approximation — does this suggest that its core contribution lies in the approximation technique rather than in the optimization principle itself?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission6450 by Reviewer odoJ

comment.value:
- Is the Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation transferable across different model architectures?
  - YAQA’s Kronecker-factored approximation is used to quantize linear layers within models. As long as a model contains linear layers, YAQA can be used to quantize linear layers.
  - If you are asking whether a set of Hessian sketches for one model can be used for another completely different model architecture, then the answer is no. **We do not see how you would be able to map layers to each other, especially if the dimensions or number of layers does not match. Doing so would imply there is a bijection between layers in different models, which obviously does not exist in almost all cases.** The only case where you might be able to reuse Hessians is between different finetunes of the same base model, such as between a base and instruct-tuned model.
- Can the “structural nilpotence degree” quantitatively predict convergence speed in real applications?
  - The SND is a bound on the number of serial steps needed to implement LDLQ. In most practical implementations, the number of steps is exactly equal to the SND, so the SND directly measures the convergence rate of LDLQ.
- Can the proposed method be applied to mixed-precision quantization?
  - Can you clarify what you mean by mixed precision quantization? **If you are referring to having a different weight bitrate than activation bitrate, all experiments in this paper use 16 bit activations with quantized weights. YAQA is a weight quantization algorithm, so naturally we did not quantize the activations.** If you are referring to using a different number of bits per layer, YAQA operates independently over layers, so there is nothing stopping one from choosing different bitrates for each layer. 
- The paper claims that the proposed method introduces no additional inference overhead — could the authors provide supporting evidence or justification for this claim?
  - Inference speed properties are determined by pre and post processing steps and the quantizer used. **YAQA only chooses an assignment among representable points in the quantized representation, so YAQA does not affect inference speed.** Analogously, the speed of multiplying two non-degenerate dense matrices is determined by the datatypes and matrix sizes, not the entries of the matrices themselves.
- The advantage of YAQA appears to mainly arise from its more accurate Hessian approximation — does this suggest that its core contribution lies in the approximation technique rather than in the optimization principle itself?
  - **There are three main contributions in YAQA: (1) the SND, which characterizes how fast we can run LDLQ, (2) theory on what makes a good Hessian sketch for LDLQ, and (3) YAQA’s Hessian sketches and fully distributed implementations of them.**
  - For the first, we show that certain structured Hessian approximations have low SNDs, which allow us to efficiently incorporate full-model information into LDLQ. For the second, we show that the closer a Hessian approximation is to the true Hessian, the lower the actual end-to-end error will be, which represents the first theoretical bound on the end-to-end error for any quantization algorithm. Finally, for the third, we provide two practical Hessian sketches that both empirically strongly outperform prior state of the art methods.
  - YAQA is equivalent to running LDLQ with a Kronecker factored Hessian approximation, so the empirical improvements in quality come from the improved Hessian sketches. However, the contributions of this paper span from theory (on convergence rates and error bounds for different Hessian sketches) to practice (implementing YAQA and state of the art empirical results for quantizing modern LLMs).

display_title: Official Review of Submission6450 by Reviewer EML8

summary.value: The paper introduces PTQ approach called YAQA which solves the issue in GPTQ and LDLQ of layerwise activation error minimization as a proxy to end to end model error. YAQA minimized the KL divergence between original model and quantized model output distribution. The paper also provides the theoretical bound on end to end quantization error and shows the cosine similarity between a Kronecker factored Hessian approximation and true Hessian. The evaluations in the paper show that YAQA improves KL error by approx 30% compared to GPTQ and LDLQ.

strengths.value:
- The paper is easy to read, well structured and clearly written. The main claims in the paper are well supported by rigorous theoretical proofs and extensive empirical evaluation.
- The paper provides novel contributions to a highly impactful area of model compression.
- The theoretical framework is strong and justifies the adoption of Kronecker factored Hessian that enables fast and symmetric I/O feedback during adaptive rounding. 
- The paper provably shows superiority over LDLQ under the low rank condition.
- The empirical results are strong. YAQA has been shown to consistently outperform LDLQ by reduction in KL div by approximately 30% margin. YAQA also has been shown to achieve lower KLD than large scale QAT Gemma-3 12B.

weaknesses.value:
- Its not clear how much is the actual quantization time cost. The paper states that YAQA adds no inference overhead and has the same asymptotic complexity as LDLQ. It would be good to show actual wall clock time comparison against LDLQ on large model since YAQA requires power iteration on model hessian.
- YAQA is provable shown to be better than LDLQ based on the assumption H_O is low rank. Could the authors show empirical evidence to support the assumption?
- The evaluations are mainly focused on W4A16 but it is not clear from the paper if YAQA can be used for 3 bit or 2 bit where rounding noise is more dominant and also more challenging setup of W4A4 where both weights and activations are low precision.
- The paper contrasts YAQA with block diagonal approximations. Could the authors provide a more detailed theoretical comparison, within the SND framework, of why the Kronecker factored structure is better than the block diagonal structure, beyond the empirical observation?

questions.value:
- LLMs are known to suffer from activation outliers in intermediate layers. Since YAQA is based on an objective to minimize KL divergence, does the inclusion of the Hessian factor (H_O​) implicitly mitigate the effect of these activation outliers. 
- Can the authors show via an ablation on if the performance gain in YAQA is due to advance power iteration or due to the symmetric form?

comment.value:
- Its not clear how much is the actual quantization time cost...
  - **Lines 300-301 and 315-316 in the paper give concrete numbers for the cost of obtaining Hessians. Section A.2 in the Appendix contains an analysis of the number of FLOPs needed for each Hessian sketch.** The cost of quantization (i.e. running the fixed point iteration) is higher than LDLQ due to the higher SND, but both are negligible in practice (under a minute per linear layer for a 8B model with an unoptimized implementation). A single set of Hessians for a model can also be reused across different quantizations of the same model, amortizing cost.
  - **It is important to note that in practice, the cost of quantization is usually not a factor in deciding which quantized model to deploy. Quantized models reap savings every time they are run, whereas quantization is a one-time fixed overhead cost.** Choosing the highest quality quantized model for a target size is more important than saving cost up front, which is one reason why people use QAT in practice despite it costing much more than PTQ.
- YAQA is provable shown to be better than LDLQ ...
  - **Figure 1 in the paper contains empirical evidence that H_O is low rank.**
- The evaluations are mainly focused on W4A16 ...
  - **Tables 1 and 4 in the paper contain extensive empirical results in 2 and 3 bit settings. YAQA significantly outperforms all baselines in these settings.** We did not evaluate YAQA in activation quantization settings since YAQA is a weight-only quantization algorithm. All the PTQ baselines (GPTQ, LDLQ, GuidedQuant, and DiscQuant) are also weight-only algorithms and the Google QAT model was evaluated in a weight-only setup.   
- The paper contrasts YAQA with block diagonal approximations ...
  - **See A.3 in the Appendix.** A block diagonal Hessian with $g$ $n \times n$ blocks has a SND of $n$ per block. A serial implementation of LDLQ with a block diagonal Hessian would have an effective SND of $gn$. In contrast, a Kronecker-factored Hessian has a SND of $m+n$, which is about $2n$ if $m \approx n$. The GuidedQuant results in the tables use $g=4$, which gives a SND around 2x YAQA. However, GuidedQuant performs worse than YAQA. Furthermore, increasing the number of blocks does not always increase performance in GuidedQuant, but does increase the SND linearly, making it much more costly than YAQA.
- LLMs are known to suffer from activation outliers in intermediate layers ... 
  - Could you concretely define what you mean by the “effect of these activation outliers?” The inclusion of $H_O$ adds another dimension of feedback during adaptive rounding. This allows the adaptive rounding algorithm to better incorporate linear feedback during rounding, some of which may be caused by over/underflow from outliers. However, there may be other effects of outliers that you have in mind that we are not aware of.
  - Much of what the wider literature considers as “effects of outliers” can be explained by the “incoherence” of the Hessian and weight matrices. There is lots of theory on the effect of incoherence and incoherence processing on the quantization error of LDLQ (see QuIP (Chee et al.), QuIP# (Tseng et al.) and Section 3 in this paper). As our theory suggests, incoherence processing empirically improves the quality of YAQA, but YAQA still outperforms all baselines even without incoherence processing (Table 6 in the Appendix). 
- Can the authors show via an ablation on if the performance gain in YAQA is due to advance power iteration or due to the symmetric form?
  - Could you clarify what you mean by “symmetric form?” If you are referring to the inclusion of $H_O$ during quantization, including H_O alone does not necessarily improve quantization. The improvement in quality is from both including $H_O$ and choosing a good estimate for $H_O$. Setting $H_O = I$ and $H_I = H_1$ reduces to running LDLQ (see L231 in the paper), which would obviously give no improvement over LDLQ. 
  - Theorem 1 in the paper describes what a “good” $H_O$ and $H_I$ look like. For YAQA to perform well, $H_O \otimes H_I$ should be directionally similar to $H$, which is the motivation behind the Hessian sketches in YAQA. Figure 3 in the paper shows an ablation on the dataset size and Hessian sketch in terms of relative cosine similarity to H. This, in conjunction with Tables 1 and 4 in the paper, form an ablation on the effect of the sketch quality on final performance. If you are interested in more empirical studies on the effect of power iteration on the cosine similarity to the true Hessian, we suggest reading https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.17748.

comment.value:
Since the discussion period was cut short before most of our reviewers had a chance to respond, we have written a summary of our paper and the discussion period:

**The core of our paper is a new LLM post-training quantization (PTQ) rounding algorithm, YAQA, that directly minimizes the end-to-end error to the original model in a principled way.** Current SOTA PTQ algorithms either only minimize the immediate local error or use heuristics to incorporate global information, both of which deliver suboptimal results. To address these issues, our paper makes three main contributions:
- First, we characterize the convergence time of adaptive rounding algorithms via the structure of their Hessian approximations. We introduce the “Structural Nilpotence Degree,” which lets us **bound the runtime of adaptive rounding.**
- We then show that the end-to-end error can be bounded by the Hessian approximation's cosine similarity to the true Hessian. This admits a natural Kronecker-factored approximation with corresponding near-optimal Hessian sketches that make YAQA **provably better than GPTQ and LDLQ.**
- Finally, we empirically show that YAQA achieves state of the art downstream results, such as **reducing the KL by >30% over prior SOTA methods** on modern hundred-billion parameter LLMs and even **achieving a lower error than Google’s latest QAT method.**

Reviewers largely agreed that our contributions were impactful and recognized that YAQA **“provides the first formal end-to-end quantization error bounds” (odoJ)** and had **strong empirical results (EML8, RfGj)**. Reviewers also found that our paper was **“easy to read, well structured, and clearly written” (EML8)**, with support from a **strong theoretical framework with rigorous proofs (EML8, u5sZ)** and **extensive empirical evaluation (u5sZ, RfGj).**

During the rebuttal period, we attempted to address all questions raised by reviewers. Unfortunately, only RfGj was able to respond before the OpenReview incident and response cutoff, **who concluded that their questions and concerns had been resolved by our response.** Our responses to the other reviewers still hold and we encourage those interested to read them. We note that **the vast majority of remaining questions raised by other reviewers were directly answered in the original text.**

In our view, YAQA makes significant strides in advancing both theory and practice in LLM quantization. **YAQA’s theory represents the first end-to-end error bounds for any quantization algorithm**, marking a pivotal step in understanding the behavior of quantization on LLMs. These bounds directly translate to a new frontier in empirical quantization quality: across a wide range of LLMs (Llama, Gemma), model sizes (1B to 70B), and quantizers (QTIP, INT4), **YAQA outperformed state of the art baselines from every quantization category (PTQ, QAT, finetuning).**

summary.value:
I have read the paper myself and have also read all reviewer comments and the full discussion thread, including the authors’ rebuttals and the subsequent exchanges.

The paper proposes YAQA, a post-training quantization (PTQ) adaptive rounding method for LLMs that directly minimizes end-to-end error (via KL divergence between the original and quantized model output distributions) using Kronecker-factored Hessian sketches, and presents theoretical bounds connecting end-to-end error to the quality (cosine similarity) of the Hessian approximation. The submission reports empirical improvements over prior PTQ baselines (e.g., LDLQ/GuidedQuant) across LLMs and bit-width settings, and includes comparisons to a QAT baseline (Google’s QAT Gemma 3) in a weight-only setup.

The the following concerns are considered as critical:

(i) The empirical evidence is not sufficiently strong. In the rebuttal, the authors claim that “YAQA outperformed state of the art baselines from every quantization category (PTQ, QAT, finetuning).” This statement appears overstated and potentially misleading, especially given that the paper does not provide comprehensive comparisons across all major categories. Although the rebuttal lists many state-of-the-art quantization approaches (GPTQ, QuIP, QuIP#, QTIP, NestQuant, SmoothQuant, AWQ, SpinQuant, QuaRot, OmniQuant, CBQ, AQLM, PV-Tuning, etc.), only a small subset of these methods are actually evaluated in the paper, leaving out several competitive and widely recognized baselines.

(ii) The rebuttal regarding LSQ is also not convincing. LSQ is a general-purpose quantization-aware training (QAT) method, not restricted to vision models, and is broadly regarded as a strong and simple baseline. Although it is proposed in 2019, it is still widely used and is cited over 1200 times. Many LLM quantization papers adopt LSQ as a standard QAT baseline. In contrast, Gemma (the Google QAT method cited by the authors) is not a quantization-focused paper; treating Gemma’s QAT setup as the primary baseline appears to select an easier comparison target rather than engaging with widely accepted QAT baselines.

Given these issues, I recommend rejection.

reviewer_concerns.value:
### Concerns addressed by the rebuttal (based strictly on the thread)

* **Quantization-time cost and Hessian sketching cost (EML8, RfGj):** The authors pointed to concrete numbers in the paper (lines 300–301 and 315–316) and additional FLOP analysis in the appendix (A.2). They also stated quantization cost is under a minute per linear layer for an 8B model with an unoptimized implementation and that Hessians can be reused across quantizations of the same model. RfGj explicitly stated they were satisfied with the answers and could find the requested details in the appendix.
* **Low-rank assumption evidence (EML8):** The authors stated that Figure 1 provides empirical evidence that (H_O) is low rank.
* **2-bit / 3-bit results (EML8):** The authors stated Tables 1 and 4 contain extensive results in 2- and 3-bit settings, and clarified that YAQA is a weight-only algorithm and therefore does not target activation quantization settings such as W4A4.
* **Mixed precision interpretation and inference overhead (odoJ):** The authors clarified their interpretation of mixed precision (quantized weights with 16-bit activations, or different per-layer bitrates) and argued YAQA does not change inference speed because it only selects among representable points under a fixed quantization format.
* **Requests for QAT comparisons (RfGj):** The authors indicated Table 3 and Section 4.1.1 include a comparison against QAT baselines, specifically Google’s QAT Gemma 3, and argued YAQA achieves lower KL divergence in the weight-only evaluation setup. RfGj later acknowledged this and indicated no further questions.
* **Generalizability to vision models (RfGj):** The authors provided a detailed rationale for focusing on LLMs and why “pure” vision model evaluation was out of scope; RfGj subsequently agreed with this justification and stated they had no further questions.

### Concerns partially solved:

* **Direct wall-clock comparison request (EML8):** While the authors referenced existing cost numbers and appendix FLOP analysis, EML8’s review specifically asked for “actual wall clock time comparison against LDLQ on large model.”
